Norwegian Semiconductor Plants Hit by Norovirus Outbreak, Disrupting Operations

A norovirus outbreak has struck the semiconductor manufacturing sector in Norway, leading to significant staffing shortages and temporary process slowdowns at multiple fabrication sites. The outbreak, first identified late last week at NordSilicon’s Kristiansand facility, has now affected at least four major plants across southern Norway, according to the Norwegian Semiconductor Industry Association (NSIA).

Symptoms have included severe gastrointestinal distress, leading to a spike in worker absenteeism. As of Tuesday, NSIA estimates that approximately 18% of the sector’s workforce is currently unable to report to work due to illness or quarantine protocols. “This is an unprecedented challenge for our members,” said NSIA General Secretary Solveig Lunde. “We are working closely with health authorities to contain the outbreak and support affected employees.”

FabSol, which operates a 24/7 foundry in Arendal, reported that several cleanroom shifts are running with skeleton crews. “We have activated our emergency continuity plan,” said FabSol’s site director Morten Skaar. “Output is down by about 30% this week, but our top priority remains staff wellbeing and rigorous sanitation.”

Production lines requiring high-density staffing have been most affected, with some assembly and testing processes temporarily suspended. Several companies have implemented staggered shifts and remote work for eligible engineering staff to limit further transmission.

The NSIA reported that no fatalities have occurred, and most affected employees are expected to recover within days. However, the ongoing nature of the outbreak has delayed some planned maintenance and ramp-up schedules. “If absenteeism continues at this level, there could be further disruption to current capacity,” said Liv Haug, a semiconductor industry analyst at Oslo Market Insights.

Industry trade union Semikraften has called for enhanced sick pay provisions and additional on-site medical support. The NSIA said it will provide further updates as the situation evolves.
